fuentes/la-situacion-de-la-clase-obrera/.texto: The Condition of the Working Class in England

Drawing on what he saw in Manchester between 1842 and 1844 and on official reports, Engels describes the housing, health, child labor and wages of English factory workers. He argues that industry concentrates workers into a class with interests opposed to the bourgeoisie and foretells a social revolution.
It is one of the first social investigations of the Industrial Revolution and the starting point of Engels's collaboration with Marx.

fuentes/manifiesto-comunista/resumen.texto: Commissioned by the Communist League and written by Marx and Engels, it was published in London in February 1848. It presents history as the history of class struggle, describes how the bourgeoisie revolutionized production and created its own gravedigger, the proletariat, and proposes abolishing private ownership of the means of production. It ends with “Workers of the world, unite!”.

fuentes/manifiesto-comunista/por_que_imp.texto: It is the most widely circulated political text of socialism and the reference program of communist parties. Its critics point out that the regimes that invoked it suppressed the freedoms the revolution promised to expand.

fuentes/el-dieciocho-brumario/titulo.texto: The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte

fuentes/el-dieciocho-brumario/resumen.texto: Marx analyzes Louis Napoleon Bonaparte's coup d'état (December 1851) as the result of the balance between classes after the revolution of 1848, with a State that seems to become independent of all of them. It opens with the line that history repeats itself “first as tragedy, then as farce”.

fuentes/el-dieciocho-brumario/por_que_im.texto: It is the model of Marxist analysis of the political conjuncture and the basis of the theory of “Bonapartism”.

fuentes/manifiesto-inaugural-de-la-ait/t.texto: Inaugural Address of the International Workingmen's Association

fuentes/manifiesto-inaugural-de-la-ait/r.texto: Written by Marx for the First International, founded in London in September 1864, it contrasts the growth of English wealth with the misery of the workers and praises the Ten Hours Act and the cooperatives. Like the Communist Manifesto, it ends by calling on the proletarians of all countries to unite; the accompanying statutes stated that the emancipation of the working classes must be achieved by the working classes themselves.

fuentes/manifiesto-inaugural-de-la-ait/p.texto: It set the program of the first international workers' organization, which brought together trade unionists, mutualists, Marxists and anarchists.

fuentes/el-capital/titulo.texto: Capital: A Critique of Political Economy

fuentes/el-capital/soporte.texto: Book (volume I; volumes II and III edited by Engels in 1885 and 1894)

fuentes/el-capital/resumen.texto: Volume I, published in Hamburg in 1867 after years of study in the British Museum library, analyzes the commodity, money and capital. It argues that profit comes from surplus value, the unpaid labor of the worker, and that competition leads to the concentration of capital and to periodic crises. Its main example is English industry.

fuentes/el-capital/por_que_importa.texto: It is the central work of Marxist economic theory. Neoclassical economics rejected its labor theory of value, and the Austrian school challenged the possibility of socialist economic calculation.

fuentes/el-capital/leer.0.titulo.texto: Volume I in English on marxists.org

fuentes/la-guerra-civil-en-francia/sopor.texto: Address of the General Council of the IWA

fuentes/la-guerra-civil-en-francia/resum.texto: Written as an address of the International a few days after the defeat of the Paris Commune, it defends the Commune's work: a militia instead of an army, and elected, recallable officials paid workers' wages. Marx concludes that the working class cannot simply take hold of the ready-made State machinery, but must replace it.

fuentes/la-guerra-civil-en-francia/por_q.texto: It turned the Commune into the model of the “dictatorship of the proletariat” to which Engels and Lenin later returned.

fuentes/critica-del-programa-de-gotha/re.texto: A critical commentary on the unification program of the German socialists, which Marx reproaches for its concessions to Lassalle. It distinguishes a first phase of communism, in which people are paid according to their labor, from a higher phase governed by “from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs”, and mentions the revolutionary dictatorship of the proletariat as a transitional period.

fuentes/critica-del-programa-de-gotha/po.texto: It is the text in which Marx comes closest to describing the future society, and it was cited in all later debates on the transition to socialism.

fuentes/anti-duhring/titulo.texto: Herr Eugen Dühring's Revolution in Science (Anti-Dühring)

fuentes/anti-duhring/soporte.texto: Book (previously serialized in the newspaper Vorwärts)

fuentes/anti-duhring/resumen.texto: A polemic against the philosopher Eugen Dühring, influential among German Social Democrats, which Engels turned into a comprehensive exposition of Marxism: philosophy, political economy and socialism. It formulates the dialectics of nature and the idea that the State “will wither away”.

fuentes/anti-duhring/por_que_importa.texto: For decades it was the main gateway to Marxism for activists, especially in its abridged version.

fuentes/del-socialismo-utopico-al-cienti.texto: Three chapters of Anti-Dühring collected at the request of Paul Lafargue. It values Saint-Simon, Fourier and Owen as forerunners, but argues that their socialism was a moral ideal, whereas Marx's is based on historical materialism and the analysis of surplus value.
It established the distinction between “utopian” and “scientific” socialism that Marxists used to judge other currents.

fuentes/el-origen-de-la-familia/titulo.texto: The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State

fuentes/el-origen-de-la-familia/resumen.texto: Based on Marx’s notes on Ancient Society (1877) by Lewis H. Morgan, which drew largely on his studies of the Iroquois, it argues that the monogamous family, private property and the state arose together with the appearance of surplus and social classes. It sees in that process “the great historical defeat of the female sex.”

fuentes/el-origen-de-la-familia/por_que_.texto: It was the basis of Marxist theory on the oppression of women and on the origin of the State. Later anthropology abandoned Morgan's evolutionary scheme on which it rests.

fuentes/ensayos-fabianos/resumen.texto: Eight lectures by members of the Fabian Society, among them Shaw, Sidney Webb and Annie Besant, published in 1889. They propose reaching socialism gradually, through suffrage, municipalities and the expansion of public services, without revolution.

fuentes/ensayos-fabianos/por_que_importa.texto: It was the manifesto of British reformist socialism and one of the doctrinal roots of the Labour Party.

fuentes/programa-de-erfurt/resumen.texto: Program of the Social Democratic Party of Germany adopted at its 1891 Erfurt congress. Its theoretical part, by Kautsky, announces the collapse of capitalism and the socialization of the means of production; its practical part, by Bernstein, calls for universal suffrage, the eight-hour day and secular schooling.

fuentes/programa-de-erfurt/por_que_impor.texto: It was the model for the parties of the Second International and showed the tension between revolutionary goal and reformist practice.

fuentes/las-premisas-del-socialismo/titu.texto: The Prerequisites of Socialism and the Tasks of Social Democracy

fuentes/las-premisas-del-socialismo/resu.texto: Bernstein argues that the middle classes are not disappearing, that crises are not worsening and that capitalism is not heading toward collapse, so socialism must come through reforms, trade unions and cooperatives, with democracy as both means and end. He sums up his position by saying that the movement is everything and the final goal nothing.

fuentes/las-premisas-del-socialismo/por_.texto: It opened the “revisionist controversy” and is the founding text of reformist social democracy. Kautsky and Luxemburg replied that it renounced socialism.

fuentes/reforma-o-revolucion/resumen.texto: A reply to Bernstein published in the Leipziger Volkszeitung and then as a pamphlet. Luxemburg argues that reforms are useful for organizing workers but cannot abolish exploitation, and that renouncing the conquest of power amounts to abandoning socialism.

fuentes/reforma-o-revolucion/por_que_imp.texto: It is the classic Marxist critique of reformism and made its author known within German Social Democracy.

fuentes/que-hacer-lenin/resumen.texto: Lenin argues that workers on their own reach only trade-union consciousness and that socialist consciousness must be brought to them “from without” by a centralized party of professional revolutionaries. He polemicizes with the “Economists”, who gave priority to wage struggles.

fuentes/que-hacer-lenin/por_que_importa.texto: Its model of a vanguard party split Bolsheviks and Mensheviks in 1903 and shaped the communist parties of the 20th century. Luxemburg and Trotsky warned at the time that it led to substituting the party for the class and the leader for the party.

fuentes/el-marxismo-y-la-cuestion-nacion.texto: Written in Vienna at Lenin's request, it defines the nation as a stable community of language, territory, economic life and culture. It rejects the non-territorial cultural autonomy of the Austro-Marxists and the Jewish Bund, and defends the right of nations to self-determination within a single workers' party.
It was the basis of Soviet nationalities policy and of the exclusion of Jews from the definition of a nation for lacking a territory.

fuentes/imperialismo-fase-superior/titul.texto: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism

fuentes/imperialismo-fase-superior/resum.texto: Written in Zurich in 1916, drawing on Hobson and Hilferding, it argues that capitalism has entered a stage of monopolies and finance capital that exports capital and divides the world into colonies. It explains the world war as a clash between imperialist powers, and the support of part of the workers for it by a privileged “labor aristocracy”.

fuentes/imperialismo-fase-superior/por_q.texto: It was the theory of imperialism of the communist and anti-imperialist movements of the 20th century.

fuentes/tesis-de-abril/resumen.texto: Ten theses that Lenin presented on returning from exile in April 1917. They call for no support for the Provisional Government, an end to the war and the transfer of “all power to the soviets”, without waiting for a long period of bourgeois democracy.

fuentes/tesis-de-abril/por_que_importa.texto: They reoriented the Bolsheviks toward the seizure of power that took place in October.

fuentes/el-estado-y-la-revolucion/resume.texto: Written underground in August and September 1917, it surveys what Marx and Engels said about the State as an instrument of class domination. It argues that the proletariat must destroy the bourgeois State, exercise its dictatorship on the model of the Commune and let the State wither away.

fuentes/el-estado-y-la-revolucion/por_qu.texto: It is the theory of the State of Leninism. Its critics contrast its Commune-type democracy with the one-party State that Lenin built.

fuentes/la-revolucion-rusa-luxemburgo/re.texto: Written in Breslau prison in 1918, it praises the boldness of the Bolsheviks but criticizes the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly and the suppression of freedoms. It states that “freedom is always the freedom of the one who thinks differently” and that without elections or a free press public life dies out and a bureaucracy rules.

fuentes/la-revolucion-rusa-luxemburgo/po.texto: It is the earliest critique of the Bolshevik regime from within revolutionary Marxism itself.

fuentes/historia-y-conciencia-de-clase/r.texto: Essays that reread Marx through Hegel: totality, the class consciousness of the proletariat and reification, whereby relations between people appear as relations between things. The Communist International condemned it and Lukács recanted.

fuentes/historia-y-conciencia-de-clase/p.texto: It is the founding text of “Western Marxism” and a direct influence on the Frankfurt School.

fuentes/siete-ensayos/titulo.texto: Seven Interpretive Essays on Peruvian Reality

fuentes/siete-ensayos/resumen.texto: Mariátegui analyzes Peru's economy, the problem of the Indian, land, education, religion, regionalism and literature. He argues that the problem of the Indian is the problem of land, held by gamonalismo, and that Andean communal traditions can connect with socialism.

fuentes/siete-ensayos/por_que_importa.texto: It is the first major Marxist interpretation of a Latin American society and a classic of indigenismo.

fuentes/cuadernos-de-la-carcel/resumen.texto: Notes written in prison on Italian history, intellectuals, culture and politics. They develop the concepts of hegemony, historic bloc, war of position and organic intellectual to explain why in the West bourgeois power rests on civil society and not only on the State.

fuentes/cuadernos-de-la-carcel/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the most influential Marxist works of the 20th century, in the European and Latin American left and in cultural studies. It is also cited by sections of the right that call for a “culture war”.

fuentes/la-revolucion-permanente/resumen.texto: Written during his exile in Turkey, it defends against Stalin the theory formulated in 1905: in backward countries the bourgeoisie cannot complete the democratic revolution, which must be led by the proletariat and extended internationally. It rejects “socialism in one country”.

fuentes/la-revolucion-permanente/por_que.texto: It is the doctrinal core of Trotskyism and the Fourth International.

fuentes/la-revolucion-traicionada/resume.texto: Written in Norway, it describes the USSR as a “degenerated workers' state”: state property remains in place, but a privileged bureaucracy headed by Stalin has expropriated the workers' political power. It predicts that this bureaucracy would either fall through a political revolution or end up restoring capitalism.

fuentes/la-revolucion-traicionada/por_qu.texto: It is the most widely read Marxist critique of Stalinism and anticipated debates on the social nature of the USSR.

fuentes/sobre-la-practica/resumen.texto: A lecture given in Yan'an arguing that knowledge arises from social practice, moves from the perceptual to the rational and is tested again in practice. It targets the dogmatism of the Moscow-trained leaders.

fuentes/sobre-la-practica/por_que_import.texto: Together with On Contradiction, it is the philosophical basis of Maoism.

fuentes/dialectica-de-la-ilustracion/sop.texto: Book (with Theodor W. Adorno; definitive edition in Amsterdam, 1947)

fuentes/dialectica-de-la-ilustracion/res.texto: Written in Californian exile by Horkheimer and Adorno, it argues that Enlightenment reason, reduced to the domination of nature, turns into myth and domination. It includes the chapter on the “culture industry” and another on antisemitism.

fuentes/dialectica-de-la-ilustracion/por.texto: It is the central work of the Frankfurt School's critical theory and one of the most influential critiques of modernity.

fuentes/la-historia-me-absolvera/resumen.texto: Fidel Castro's self-defense speech at the trial for the attack on the Moncada Barracks, on 16 October 1953. It denounces Batista's dictatorship and proposes a program of agrarian reform, restoration of the 1940 Constitution and nationalizations.

fuentes/la-historia-me-absolvera/por_que.texto: It became the program of the 26th of July Movement and a founding text of the Cuban Revolution.

fuentes/informe-secreto-de-jruschov/titu.texto: On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences (Secret Speech)

fuentes/informe-secreto-de-jruschov/resu.texto: Speech by Nikita Khrushchev to the 20th Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, on 25 February 1956. It denounces the cult of Stalin, the deportations and the executions of party members during the Great Purge, without questioning the one-party system.

fuentes/informe-secreto-de-jruschov/por_.texto: It launched “de-Stalinization”, caused crises in communist parties around the world and preceded the 1956 uprisings in Poland and Hungary.

fuentes/programa-de-bad-godesberg/resume.texto: Program adopted by German Social Democracy in November 1959. It abandons Marxism as official doctrine, accepts the market economy (“competition as far as possible, planning as far as necessary”) and national defense, and presents the party as a party of the whole people.

fuentes/programa-de-bad-godesberg/por_qu.texto: It marked the shift of European social democracy from the goal of socialism to the reform of capitalism and the welfare state.

fuentes/la-guerra-de-guerrillas/resumen.texto: A manual based on the experience of the Sierra Maestra. It argues that there is no need to wait for all the conditions for revolution to be in place, because the insurrectionary foco can create them, and that in Latin America the terrain of armed struggle is the countryside.

fuentes/la-guerra-de-guerrillas/por_que_.texto: It inspired Latin American guerrillas of the 1960s and 1970s, including Guevara's own in Bolivia; most were defeated.

fuentes/el-socialismo-y-el-hombre-en-cub.texto: A letter to Carlos Quijano, editor of the Uruguayan weekly Marcha, published in March 1965. It argues that socialism requires creating a “new man” driven by moral rather than material incentives, with the vanguard and voluntary labor as its driving forces.
It sums up the revolutionary ethics of Guevarism and its commitment to the transformation of consciousness.

fuentes/libro-rojo-de-mao/titulo.texto: Quotations from Chairman Mao Tse-tung (Little Red Book)

fuentes/libro-rojo-de-mao/resumen.texto: A selection of sayings from Mao's writings and speeches, compiled by the People's Liberation Army at Lin Biao's initiative. Hundreds of millions of copies were distributed and its study was compulsory during the Cultural Revolution.

fuentes/libro-rojo-de-mao/por_que_import.texto: It is one of the most printed books of the 20th century and an instrument of Mao's personality cult.

fuentes/el-hombre-unidimensional/resumen.texto: Marcuse argues that advanced industrial societies, both capitalist and Soviet, integrate individuals through consumption, technology and the media, and neutralize critical thought and opposition. He looks for the force of change among the marginalized and the students.

fuentes/el-hombre-unidimensional/por_que.texto: It was one of the key books of the New Left and of the 1968 student movement.

fuentes/pedagogia-del-oprimido/soporte.texto: Book (first edition in Spanish and English, 1970)

fuentes/pedagogia-del-oprimido/resumen.texto: Freire criticizes “banking” education, which deposits knowledge in passive students, and proposes a dialogical, problem-posing education in which the oppressed become aware of their situation in order to transform it.

fuentes/pedagogia-del-oprimido/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the most cited books on pedagogy in the world and the basis of Latin American popular education.

fuentes/el-poder-de-los-sin-poder/resume.texto: Havel describes the Czechoslovak communist regime as “post-totalitarian”: it no longer rests on terror but on everyone's ritual participation in a shared lie, like the greengrocer who puts a sign with slogans in his shop window. He proposes “living in truth” as a form of resistance.

fuentes/el-poder-de-los-sin-poder/por_qu.texto: It circulated clandestinely and became a reference text for dissidents in Eastern Europe, including those of Solidarity in Poland.

fuentes/declaracion-de-arusha/resumen.texto: Declaration of Tanzania's ruling party drafted by Nyerere in February 1967. It defines African socialism (ujamaa) as self-reliance based on agriculture and communal life, and announces the nationalization of banks and large companies.

fuentes/declaracion-de-arusha/por_que_im.texto: It was the most cited example of African socialism. The ujamaa villages, with forced relocations from 1973, did not meet their economic targets and Tanzania abandoned them in the 1980s.

fuentes/que-es-la-propiedad/resumen.texto: Proudhon answers “property is theft”: property that allows one to collect rent, interest or profit without working is an appropriation of other people's labor, though he defends possession of what each person uses. He declares himself an “anarchist”, a supporter of an order without government.

fuentes/que-es-la-propiedad/por_que_impo.texto: It is the founding text of anarchism as a political current. Marx praised it at first and later criticized it in The Poverty of Philosophy (1847).

fuentes/el-unico-y-su-propiedad/resumen.texto: Stirner rejects all the “fixed ideas” imposed on the individual, such as God, the State, humanity, morality or society, and proposes that each person assert himself as a “unique one” in voluntary unions of egoists. He criticizes Feuerbach and the socialists for replacing God with another abstraction.

fuentes/el-unico-y-su-propiedad/por_que_.texto: It is the reference work of individualist anarchism and philosophical egoism. Marx and Engels devoted a large part of The German Ideology to it.

fuentes/el-unico-y-su-propiedad/leer.0.t.texto: English translation (The Ego and His Own) on Project Gutenberg

fuentes/estatismo-y-anarquia/resumen.texto: Bakunin contrasts the social revolution of the Slavic and Latin peoples with the Prussian State and Marxism. He warns that the “dictatorship of the proletariat” would be the rule of a minority of former workers turned into a new ruling class.

fuentes/estatismo-y-anarquia/por_que_imp.texto: It is his longest political work and the most cited anarchist critique of Marxism.

fuentes/dios-y-el-estado/resumen.texto: A fragment of an 1871 manuscript published in 1882 by Carlo Cafiero and Élisée Reclus. It argues that the idea of God implies the abdication of human reason and freedom and justifies the authority of the State; it inverts Voltaire's saying: “if God really existed, it would be necessary to abolish him”.

fuentes/dios-y-el-estado/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the most translated anarchist texts and one of the most widely circulated among workers in Europe and the Americas.

fuentes/la-conquista-del-pan/resumen.texto: Kropotkin sets out anarchist communism: expropriating the wealth produced in common and distributing it according to needs, in a society of federated communes without a State or wages. He discusses how to organize food, housing and work after the revolution.

fuentes/la-conquista-del-pan/por_que_imp.texto: It was the key book of working-class anarchism in Europe and the Americas, including the Río de la Plata and the Spain of the CNT.

fuentes/el-reino-de-dios-esta-en-vosotro.texto: The Kingdom of God Is Within You
Book (published in Germany because of Russian censorship)

Tolstoy argues that the Sermon on the Mount commands not to resist evil with violence, and that this requires refusing military service, oaths and obedience to a State based on force. He accuses the Churches of having betrayed that message.
It is the central text of Christian anarchism and modern pacifism; Gandhi said it had “overwhelmed” him.

fuentes/el-apoyo-mutuo/titulo.texto: Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution

fuentes/el-apoyo-mutuo/resumen.texto: Against the reading of Darwin as a “struggle of all against all”, Kropotkin gathers examples of cooperation among animals, in “savage” societies, in the medieval village and in modern guilds and trade unions. He concludes that mutual aid is a factor of evolution as important as competition.

fuentes/el-apoyo-mutuo/por_que_importa.texto: It gave anarchism a naturalistic foundation and influenced the biology of cooperation and communitarian thought.

fuentes/el-apoyo-mutuo/leer.0.titulo.texto: Original English text at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/reflexiones-sobre-la-violencia/r.texto: Sorel defends proletarian violence and the general strike as a mobilizing “myth” that keeps the division between classes alive, against parliamentary socialism. He values the heroism and morality of the producers against bourgeois decadence.

fuentes/reflexiones-sobre-la-violencia/p.texto: It influenced revolutionary syndicalism and also Mussolini and early Italian fascism.

fuentes/programa-del-partido-liberal-mex.texto: Program of the Mexican Liberal Party

Published on 1 July 1906 by the party's board in exile, chaired by Ricardo Flores Magón. It calls for no reelection, the eight-hour day, a minimum wage, the prohibition of child labor, secular education and the distribution of idle lands.
It anticipated demands that the Mexican Revolution took up in the Constitution of 1917.

fuentes/anarquismo-y-otros-ensayos/resum.texto: Goldman's lectures on anarchism, political violence, patriotism, prison, the traffic in women, woman suffrage and marriage. She criticizes suffragism for trusting the state and defends women's emancipation in their personal lives.

fuentes/anarquismo-y-otros-ensayos/por_q.texto: It brings together the American version of anarchism, which combined the critique of the state with sexual freedom and feminism.

fuentes/anarquismo-y-otros-ensayos/leer..texto: Original English text at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/la-democracia-en-america/resumen.texto: Drawing on his 1831-1832 journey, Tocqueville studies equality of conditions as a feature of American society: federalism, associations, the press, religion and mores. He warns about the “tyranny of the majority” and about a soft despotism of a tutelary state over isolated individuals; he also describes the situation of slaves and of Indigenous peoples.

fuentes/la-democracia-en-america/por_que.texto: It is a classic of liberalism and political science, cited by liberals and conservatives alike.

fuentes/la-democracia-en-america/leer.0..texto: Volume I in English at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/la-democracia-en-america/leer.1..texto: Volume II in English at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/la-sujecion-de-la-mujer/resumen.texto: Mill, who wrote it under the influence of Harriet Taylor, argues that the legal subordination of the wife to the husband is a remnant of the law of the strongest and an obstacle to human progress. He calls for equality before the law, access to education and the professions, and women's suffrage, which he had proposed as a member of Parliament in 1867.

fuentes/la-sujecion-de-la-mujer/por_que_.texto: It is one of the first arguments by a male philosopher in favor of equality between the sexes and was widely read by the suffrage movement.

fuentes/la-sujecion-de-la-mujer/leer.0.t.texto: Original English text at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/que-es-una-nacion/resumen.texto: Renan rejects defining the nation by race, language, religion or geography, as German authors argued regarding Alsace-Lorraine. He defines it as a spiritual principle: a legacy of shared memories and the present will to live together, “a daily plebiscite”; he adds that the nation also requires forgetting.

fuentes/que-es-una-nacion/por_que_import.texto: It is the classic formulation of the civic and voluntary idea of the nation, as opposed to the ethnic one.

fuentes/degeneracion-nordau/resumen.texto: Nordau presents fin-de-siècle artists and writers, such as Wagner, Ibsen, Nietzsche, Tolstoy or Zola, as symptoms of a physical and nervous “degeneration” of modern civilization, using the medical categories of the time. It was a bestseller in several languages.

fuentes/degeneracion-nordau/por_que_impo.texto: It shows the thinking about decadence that surrounded early Zionism. The Nazis took up the idea of degeneration in their campaign against “degenerate art”, although Nordau was Jewish and a Zionist.

fuentes/altneuland/resumen.texto: Novel in which two travelers visit Palestine in 1902 and return in 1923 to find a modern, cooperative and technological Jewish society, with equal rights for Arabs and women's suffrage. It bears the motto “If you will it, it is no legend”.

fuentes/altneuland/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the liberal and tolerant project Herzl envisioned; Ahad Ha'am criticized it for lacking Jewish culture, and Tel Aviv took its name from the Hebrew translation of the title.

fuentes/cuestion-nacional-y-lucha-de-cla.texto: The National Question and the Class Struggle

Borochov applies historical materialism to the Jewish question: each nation's conditions of production define its class struggle, and the Jews, pushed into marginal occupations, have an “inverted” social structure. He concludes that they need a territorial base of their own to normalize their economy and their class struggle.
It was the theoretical foundation of the socialist Zionism of Poale Zion, one of the roots of Israeli Labor.

fuentes/ley-del-retorno/resumen.texto: Law passed by the Knesset on 5 July 1950 that recognizes the right of every Jew to immigrate to Israel and obtain citizenship. A 1970 amendment extended the right to the children, grandchildren and spouses of Jews and defined as Jewish a person born to a Jewish mother or who has converted and does not profess another religion.

fuentes/ley-del-retorno/por_que_importa.texto: It is the legal expression of the idea of Israel as the home of all Jews. Its Palestinian critics contrast it with the refusal to allow the return of the 1948 refugees.

fuentes/programa-del-nsdap/titulo.texto: 25-Point Program of the National Socialist Party

fuentes/programa-del-nsdap/resumen.texto: Program presented by Hitler at the Hofbräuhaus beer hall in Munich on 24 February 1920 and drafted with Anton Drexler and Gottfried Feder. It calls for the union of all Germans, the annulment of the Treaty of Versailles, the exclusion of Jews from citizenship and the expulsion of recent immigrants, along with measures against finance capital.

fuentes/programa-del-nsdap/por_que_impor.texto: It anticipates the antisemitic policy that the regime applied from 1933, beginning with the Nuremberg Laws.

fuentes/programa-del-nsdap/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation of Nuremberg document 1708-PS (Avalon Project)

fuentes/mi-lucha/resumen.texto: Written largely in Landsberg prison after the failed putsch of 1923, it mixes autobiography and program. It sets out a racist view of history as a struggle between races, presents the Jews as a world enemy allied with Marxism, and demands “living space” in the East for Germany.

fuentes/mi-lucha/por_que_importa.texto: It is a key document for understanding Nazi ideology, the war of conquest in the East and the Holocaust. In 2016 the Institute for Contemporary History in Munich published an annotated critical edition.

fuentes/manifiesto-de-los-intelectuales-.texto: Drafted by Gentile after a congress of fascist culture in Bologna and published on 21 April 1925. It presents fascism as a religious and moral movement that subordinates the individual to the state and justifies the violence of the squadristi as a regenerating force.
It was the first attempt to give fascism a philosophical justification and prompted Croce's response.

Croce's response to Gentile, published on 1 May 1925 and signed by liberal, socialist and Catholic intellectuals. It rejects the mixing of politics and culture and defends freedom, the liberal tradition of the Risorgimento and the independence of science and art from the state.
It was the main public stand of Italian culture against fascism before the full dictatorship.

fuentes/doctrina-del-fascismo/resumen.texto: Article signed by Mussolini in the Enciclopedia Italiana, whose philosophical part was written by Gentile. It defines fascism as a spiritual conception in which the state is absolute and nothing exists outside it; it rejects liberalism, democracy and socialism, and exalts war and expansion.

fuentes/doctrina-del-fascismo/por_que_im.texto: It is the official definition the regime gave of itself, with its claim to the “totalitarian” state, a term previously used by its opponents that later became an analytical category.

fuentes/el-concepto-de-lo-politico/resum.texto: Schmitt defines the political by the distinction between friend and enemy, with the real possibility of combat as its horizon. He criticizes liberalism for trying to dissolve the political into economics and ethics, and for denying that the state must decide who the enemy is.

fuentes/el-concepto-de-lo-politico/por_q.texto: It is one of the most influential critiques of parliamentary liberalism. Its author supported the Nazi regime from 1933, and the work was taken up both by the right and by left-wing authors such as Mouffe.

fuentes/ley-habilitante/resumen.texto: Passed by the Reichstag on 23 March 1933, with the Communists already arrested or banned and with the Social Democrats casting the only votes against. It allows Hitler's government to enact laws, even ones contrary to the Constitution, without parliament.

fuentes/ley-habilitante/por_que_importa.texto: It was the legal basis of the Nazi dictatorship and is the classic example of a democracy voting for its own abolition.

fuentes/ley-habilitante/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation of Nuremberg document 2001-PS (Avalon Project)

fuentes/leyes-de-nuremberg/resumen.texto: Two laws passed on 15 September 1935 at the Nazi party congress: the citizenship law, which reserved citizenship for those of “German blood”, and the law for the protection of blood, which prohibited marriages and relations between Jews and non-Jews. Later decrees defined who was Jewish according to their grandparents.

fuentes/leyes-de-nuremberg/por_que_impor.texto: They gave legal form to the exclusion of German Jews, which ended in deportation and extermination.

fuentes/leyes-de-nuremberg/leer.0.titulo.texto: Law for the Protection of Blood, document 2000-PS (Avalon Project)

fuentes/la-logica-de-la-investigacion-ci.texto: Popper argues that scientific theories cannot be verified by induction but only subjected to tests that could refute them: a theory is scientific if it is falsifiable. He thus rejects the Vienna Circle's criterion of meaning.
It is a central work of 20th-century philosophy of science and the epistemological basis of his later critique of Marxism and psychoanalysis.

fuentes/la-sociedad-abierta/titulo.texto: The Open Society and Its Enemies

fuentes/la-sociedad-abierta/soporte.texto: Book in two volumes (written in New Zealand)

fuentes/la-sociedad-abierta/resumen.texto: Popper criticizes Plato, Hegel and Marx as theorists of “historicism”, the belief in laws of history that justify total social engineering. He defends the “open society”, where governments can be changed without violence and reforms are tested and corrected piecemeal.

fuentes/la-sociedad-abierta/por_que_impo.texto: It was one of the most influential defenses of liberal democracy during the Cold War. Specialists in Plato and in Hegel considered it an unfair reading of those authors.

fuentes/los-origenes-del-totalitarismo/r.texto: Arendt traces modern antisemitism and European imperialism as antecedents, and analyzes Nazism and Stalinism as a new form of domination based on ideology, terror and concentration camps, which destroys human plurality and makes people “superfluous”.

fuentes/los-origenes-del-totalitarismo/p.texto: It is the founding work of the theory of totalitarianism. Its critics disputed the equation of Nazism with Stalinism and its reading of later communist regimes.

fuentes/dos-conceptos-de-libertad/resume.texto: Inaugural lecture at Oxford that distinguishes negative liberty, being free from interference, from positive liberty, being one's own master. He warns that positive liberty, in the name of a “true self”, can justify forcing individuals to be free, as in totalitarian regimes, and defends value pluralism.

fuentes/dos-conceptos-de-libertad/por_qu.texto: It is one of the most cited texts of 20th-century liberal political philosophy.

fuentes/hind-swaraj/titulo.texto: Hind Swaraj or Indian Home Rule

fuentes/hind-swaraj/resumen.texto: Written in ten days aboard a ship from London to South Africa, in the form of a dialogue between a reader and an editor. It argues that India will not be freed by expelling the British in order to copy their industrial civilization, but through moral self-rule, nonviolent resistance and the simple life of the villages.

fuentes/hind-swaraj/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most complete exposition of Gandhi's program; the British banned the Gujarati edition in India in 1910.

fuentes/hind-swaraj/leer.0.titulo.texto: The author's English translation (PDF) at mkgandhi.org

fuentes/discurso-sobre-el-colonialismo/r.texto: Césaire argues that colonization “decivilized” the colonizer and that Nazism applied to Europeans methods that Europe had used in the colonies. He dismantles the idea of the civilizing mission and criticizes the intellectuals who justified it.

fuentes/discurso-sobre-el-colonialismo/p.texto: It is a founding text of anticolonial and postcolonial thought.

fuentes/piel-negra-mascaras-blancas/resu.texto: Fanon uses the tools of psychiatry and phenomenology to analyze how colonial racism leads Black people in the Antilles to internalize the white gaze, in language, love and identity.

fuentes/piel-negra-mascaras-blancas/por_.texto: It is a classic of studies on racism and postcolonial identity.

fuentes/brown-contra-junta-de-educacion/.texto: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka
Supreme Court of the United States

Unanimous Supreme Court ruling of 17 May 1954, written by Chief Justice Earl Warren. It declared racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional and abandoned, for education, the “separate but equal” doctrine of Plessy v. Ferguson (1896); in 1955 it ordered its implementation “with all deliberate speed”.
It was the legal starting point of the civil rights movement, although many southern states resisted integration for years.
Decision and transcript at the U.S. National Archives

fuentes/carta-de-la-libertad/resumen.texto: Adopted on 26 June 1955 in Kliptown by the Congress of the People, which brought together the African National Congress and Indian, Coloured and white organizations. It begins: “South Africa belongs to all who live in it, black and white” and calls for equal rights, the vote for all and the redistribution of land and wealth.

fuentes/carta-de-la-libertad/por_que_imp.texto: It was the program of the African National Congress during the struggle against apartheid; the government used it to charge 156 leaders with treason in 1956.

fuentes/los-condenados-de-la-tierra/resu.texto: Written during the Algerian War, it argues that colonialism is violence and that the violence of the colonized is a way of recovering dignity and forging the nation. It also warns against national bourgeoisies that inherit the colonial state and use it for their own benefit.

fuentes/los-condenados-de-la-tierra/por_.texto: It was a reference book for Third World liberation movements and for Black Power. Its critics, such as Arendt in On Violence, objected to its justification of violence.

fuentes/carta-desde-la-carcel-de-birming.texto: Written on 16 April 1963 while King was jailed for demonstrating, it replies to eight white clergymen who had called for patience. It defends nonviolent civil disobedience against unjust laws and criticizes the “white moderate” who prefers order to justice; it says that “injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere”.
It is the most cited defense of civil disobedience in the 20th century.

fuentes/tengo-un-sueno/resumen.texto: Speech delivered on 28 August 1963 at the Lincoln Memorial, during the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. It calls for fulfilling the promise of equality in the Declaration of Independence and expresses the dream that his children will be judged by their character and not by the color of their skin.

fuentes/tengo-un-sueno/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the best-known speeches in U.S. history and contributed to the passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

fuentes/estoy-preparado-para-morir/resum.texto: Mandela's statement from the dock at the Rivonia Trial, on 20 April 1964. He explains why the African National Congress turned to sabotage after decades of nonviolent struggle and ends by saying that the ideal of a democratic and free society is one for which he is prepared to die.

fuentes/estoy-preparado-para-morir/por_q.texto: It made Mandela the world figure of the struggle against apartheid.

fuentes/el-voto-o-la-bala/resumen.texto: Speech of 3 April 1964 in Cleveland, shortly after Malcolm X left the Nation of Islam. He calls on African Americans to use the vote and Black nationalism to control their community, and warns that, if the vote continues to be denied to them, the bullet will remain.

fuentes/el-voto-o-la-bala/por_que_import.texto: It sums up his turn toward political action and his differences with King's nonviolence.

fuentes/ley-de-derechos-civiles-de-1964/.texto: Law signed by Lyndon B. Johnson on 2 July 1964, after a long blockade by southern senators. It prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin in public places, employment and federal programs, and ends legal segregation in the South.
It was the main legislative achievement of the civil rights movement, completed the following year by the Voting Rights Act.
Act and transcript at the U.S. National Archives

fuentes/neocolonialismo-nkrumah/titulo.texto: Neo-Colonialism, the Last Stage of Imperialism

fuentes/neocolonialismo-nkrumah/resumen.texto: Nkrumah, who borrows Lenin's title, argues that formally independent African states remain controlled by foreign capital, investment and aid from the former powers and the United States. He proposes the political unity of Africa as the response.

fuentes/neocolonialismo-nkrumah/por_que_.texto: It popularized the concept of neocolonialism; the United States officially protested the book and Nkrumah was overthrown the following year.

fuentes/declaracion-de-los-derechos-de-l.texto: Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen

It rewrites the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man article by article to include women. It states that “woman is born free and remains equal to man in rights” and that, if she has the right to mount the scaffold, she must also have the right to mount the rostrum.
It is one of the first demands for women's political equality. The Revolution did not take it up and its author was guillotined in 1793.

fuentes/vindicacion-de-los-derechos-de-l.texto: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman

A response to those who, like Talleyrand and Rousseau, wanted only a domestic education for women. Wollstonecraft argues that women appear inferior because of a lack of education and not by nature, and calls for a rational education for them that would make them citizens and equal companions.
It is one of the founding works of feminist philosophy.
Original English text at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/declaracion-de-seneca-falls/resu.texto: Drafted by Stanton on the model of the Declaration of Independence (“all men and women are created equal”), it lists women's grievances: no vote, no property after marriage, no access to university. It was signed by one hundred people, 68 women and 32 men, among them Frederick Douglass.

fuentes/declaracion-de-seneca-falls/por_.texto: It is the founding document of the women's rights movement in the United States; the demand for the vote, the most debated, was achieved in 1920.

fuentes/declaracion-de-seneca-falls/leer.texto: Text on the U.S. National Park Service website

fuentes/el-segundo-sexo/resumen.texto: Beauvoir analyzes, from an existentialist standpoint, how biology, psychoanalysis, Marxism, history and myths made woman the “Other” of man. Her phrase “one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman” distinguishes the biological from the socially constructed.

fuentes/el-segundo-sexo/por_que_importa.texto: It is the reference work of feminism in the second half of the 20th century. The Vatican placed it on the Index of Forbidden Books.

fuentes/la-mistica-de-la-feminidad/resum.texto: Drawing on surveys of her former college classmates, Friedan describes “the problem that has no name”: the dissatisfaction of educated middle-class women confined to the home by an ideal of femininity spread by advertising, magazines and psychology.

fuentes/la-mistica-de-la-feminidad/por_q.texto: It is considered the start of second-wave feminism in the United States. Critics pointed out that it spoke only of white middle-class women.

fuentes/la-tecnica-ellul/resumen.texto: Ellul argues that technique, understood as the search for the most efficient method in every field, has become autonomous: it develops according to its own logic, absorbs the economy, the state and human life, and admits no external moral judgment.

fuentes/la-tecnica-ellul/por_que_importa.texto: It is a classic of the critique of technology; it influenced environmentalism and was also read by Kaczynski.

fuentes/primavera-silenciosa/soporte.texto: Book (first published in The New Yorker)

fuentes/primavera-silenciosa/resumen.texto: Carson documents how DDT and other synthetic pesticides accumulate in the food chain, kill birds and fish and threaten human health, and accuses the chemical industry and the government of spreading them without studying their effects.

fuentes/primavera-silenciosa/por_que_imp.texto: It gave rise to modern environmentalism and led to the ban on agricultural use of DDT in the United States (1972). The chemical industry attacked it, and some critics attribute exaggerations about cancer to it.

fuentes/la-tragedia-de-los-comunes/resum.texto: Hardin argues that when a resource is open to all, each user has an interest in overexploiting it even if that destroys it for everyone, as in a common pasture. He applies the argument to population growth and proposes “mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon”.

fuentes/la-tragedia-de-los-comunes/por_q.texto: The concept is used in economics and ecology. Elinor Ostrom showed that many communities manage common goods without destroying them, and Hardin himself admitted he was talking about unregulated resources.

fuentes/los-limites-del-crecimiento/sopo.texto: Report to the Club of Rome

fuentes/los-limites-del-crecimiento/resu.texto: An MIT team used the World3 computer model to simulate the interaction of population, industrial output, food, resources and pollution. In the business-as-usual scenario, growth ran up against the planet's limits and collapsed during the 21st century.

fuentes/los-limites-del-crecimiento/por_.texto: It was the first major public debate on the ecological limits to growth. Economists criticized it for underestimating technology and prices; later reviews found that real-world data closely tracked the baseline scenario until the early 21st century.

fuentes/los-limites-del-crecimiento/leer.texto: Report page on the Club of Rome website

fuentes/nuestro-futuro-comun/soporte.texto: Report of the World Commission on Environment and Development

fuentes/nuestro-futuro-comun/resumen.texto: Report of the UN commission chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland. It defines sustainable development as development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own, and links environmental protection with the fight against poverty.

fuentes/nuestro-futuro-comun/por_que_imp.texto: Its definition of sustainable development became the official formula of international environmental policy and paved the way for the 1992 Earth Summit.

fuentes/nuestro-futuro-comun/leer.0.titu.texto: Full report (PDF) on the UN website

fuentes/la-sociedad-industrial-y-su-futu.texto: Manifesto published by The Washington Post and The New York Times

A text of some 35,000 words arguing that the Industrial Revolution was a disaster for humanity, that the technological system destroys human autonomy and nature and cannot be reformed, and therefore calling for a revolution against it; it includes an attack on “leftism”. Kaczynski demanded its publication in exchange for halting the bombings, and the newspapers published it on 19 September 1995 at the FBI's request.

It is preserved as a document of a criminal case: his brother David recognized the style, which led to Kaczynski's arrest in 1996 and his life sentence for bombs that killed three people and injured twenty-three. His ideas derive largely from Ellul and other critics of technology, who rejected violence.
Archived copy (Internet Archive) of the text published by The Washington Post in 1995

fuentes/quadragesimo-anno/resumen.texto: Encyclical of 15 May 1931, forty years after Rerum novarum. It rejects both economic liberalism and socialism, criticizes the concentration of economic power and formulates the principle of subsidiarity: what smaller communities can do should not be absorbed by the state. It proposes cooperation between classes through professional bodies.

fuentes/quadragesimo-anno/por_que_import.texto: It develops Catholic social teaching. Its corporatism was invoked by authoritarian regimes such as those of Salazar and Dollfuss, and subsidiarity passed into European Union law.

fuentes/quadragesimo-anno/leer.0.titulo.texto: Spanish text on the Vatican website

fuentes/teologia-de-la-liberacion/resume.texto: Gutiérrez proposes thinking about faith from the practice of liberating the poor of Latin America, with the “preferential option for the poor” and dependency analysis as tools. He draws on the Medellín episcopal conference (1968), which denounced “institutionalized violence”.

fuentes/teologia-de-la-liberacion/por_qu.texto: It gave liberation theology its name. The Vatican, under Cardinal Ratzinger, criticized its use of Marxist analysis in 1984, and the papacy of Francis rehabilitated its authors.

fuentes/laudato-si/titulo.texto: Laudato si': On Care for Our Common Home

fuentes/laudato-si/resumen.texto: Encyclical signed on 24 May 2015 and published in June. It accepts the scientific consensus on global warming, criticizes the “technocratic paradigm” and consumerism, and proposes an “integral ecology” that links care for the environment with justice for the poor.

fuentes/laudato-si/por_que_importa.texto: It is the first encyclical devoted to the environment and was published before the Paris climate agreement.

fuentes/laudato-si/leer.0.titulo.texto: Spanish text on the Vatican website

fuentes/hegemonia-y-estrategia-socialist.texto: Laclau and Mouffe abandon the primacy of the working class and the economic determinism of Marxism. Drawing on Gramsci and poststructuralism, they argue that political identities are built by articulating diverse demands (labor, feminist, environmentalist, anti-racist) and propose a “radical and plural democracy”.
It founded “post-Marxism” and the Essex school of political discourse theory. Orthodox Marxists accused it of dissolving class analysis.

fuentes/el-fin-de-la-historia/resumen.texto: Article published in the summer of 1989, before the fall of the Berlin Wall. Drawing on Alexandre Kojève's Hegelian reading, it argues that the failure of fascism and communism showed that liberal democracy and the market economy were the end point of humanity's ideological evolution, even though conflicts would continue.

fuentes/el-fin-de-la-historia/por_que_im.texto: It was the most debated interpretation of the end of the Cold War. Huntington responded with the clash of civilizations, and critics later pointed to the rise of nationalism, Islamism and China.

fuentes/el-fin-de-la-historia-y-el-ultim.texto: The End of History and the Last Man

Expands on the 1989 article: modern science pushes toward capitalism and the struggle for recognition (thymos) toward liberal democracy. It asks, with Nietzsche, whether the satisfied “last man” of that society will not seek new conflicts to assert himself.
It became the symbol of the liberal optimism of the 1990s and a target of criticism after 11 September.

fuentes/imperio-hardt-negri/resumen.texto: Hardt and Negri argue that globalization replaced the imperialism of nation-states with a decentralized “Empire”, a network of power with no territorial center that brings together states, international organizations and corporations. They see the “multitude”, a network of singularities, as the subject of resistance.

fuentes/imperio-hardt-negri/por_que_impo.texto: It was a key reference for the alter-globalization movement. The 2001 attacks and the Iraq War led its critics to stress the continuing power of the United States.

fuentes/la-razon-populista/resumen.texto: Laclau argues that populism is not an anomaly but a logic of politics: unmet demands are articulated in a “chain of equivalence” against a common power, and an empty signifier, often a leader, unifies them as “the people”.

fuentes/la-razon-populista/por_que_impor.texto: It is the main theory of left-wing populism and has been used to think about Kirchnerism, Chavismo and Podemos. Its liberal critics object that it justifies polarization and the concentration of power in the leader.

personas/marx/resumen.texto: German philosopher and economist who, in exile in London from 1849, wrote The Communist Manifesto (1848) with Engels and later Capital (1867). His theory of class struggle and his critique of capitalism founded Marxism, which inspired socialist parties and the communist states of the 20th century.

personas/engels/resumen.texto: Son of textile industrialists, he described working-class life in Manchester (1845) and was Marx's collaborator and financial supporter. After Marx's death he edited volumes II and III of Capital and popularized Marxism in Anti-Dühring and The Origin of the Family.

personas/lassalle/resumen.texto: In 1863 he founded the General German Workers' Association, Germany's first workers' party, with a program of universal suffrage and state-supported cooperatives. His movement merged with that of Bebel and Liebknecht at Gotha (1875), whose program Marx criticized.

personas/kautsky/resumen.texto: Leading theorist of German Social Democracy and the Second International, he wrote the doctrinal section of the Erfurt Program (1891). He defended Marxist orthodoxy against Bernstein and later condemned the Bolshevik dictatorship, for which Lenin called him a “renegade”.

personas/bernstein/resumen.texto: German Social Democrat who, from exile in London, argued that capitalism was not heading toward collapse and that socialism would come through gradual reforms and the parliamentary road. His “revisionism” (1899) opened the great debate of the Second International.

personas/rosa-luxemburgo/resumen.texto: Polish-German Marxist who answered Bernstein in Reform or Revolution (1899) and defended the mass strike. She opposed the 1914 war, founded the Spartacus League and criticized the lack of freedoms under the Bolshevik regime; she was murdered by the Freikorps in Berlin in January 1919.

personas/lenin/resumen.texto: Leader of the Bolshevik faction, he theorized a party of professional revolutionaries (What Is to Be Done?, 1902) and led the seizure of power in October 1917. He ruled Soviet Russia until his death with a one-party regime that repressed the opposition, and founded the Communist International.

personas/trotsky/resumen.texto: Chairman of the Petrograd Soviet in 1905 and in 1917, he organized the October insurrection and the Red Army. Defeated by Stalin, he was expelled from the USSR in 1929, denounced the Soviet bureaucracy and founded the Fourth International (1938); an agent of Stalin assassinated him in Mexico in 1940.

personas/stalin/resumen.texto: General Secretary of the Communist Party from 1922, he prevailed over his rivals after Lenin's death and ruled the USSR until 1953. He drove forced collectivization and rapid industrialization, and under his rule the Great Purge and the Gulag camp system caused millions of deaths.

personas/gramsci/resumen.texto: Co-founder of the Communist Party of Italy (1921), he was imprisoned by the fascist regime in 1926. In the Prison Notebooks he developed the concept of hegemony: a class's dominance rests as much on cultural consent as on force.

personas/lukacs/resumen.texto: Hungarian philosopher, commissar for culture of the Hungarian Soviet Republic of 1919. History and Class Consciousness (1923) renewed Marxism with the concepts of reification and class consciousness and influenced the Frankfurt School.

personas/mariategui/resumen.texto: Peruvian journalist who founded the magazine Amauta (1926) and the Socialist Party of Peru (1928). In his Seven Essays he applied Marxism to Andean reality and saw the Indigenous community as a basis for socialism.

personas/mao/resumen.texto: Leader of the Chinese Communist Party, he adapted Marxism-Leninism to a revolution based on the peasantry and proclaimed the People's Republic in 1949. The Great Leap Forward caused a famine with tens of millions of deaths, and the Cultural Revolution persecuted millions of people.

personas/che-guevara/resumen.texto: Rosario-born physician who joined Fidel Castro's guerrillas and was Cuba's Minister of Industries. He theorized the guerrilla foco and the “New Man”; he was executed in Bolivia in 1967 after being captured. His supporters see him as a revolutionary symbol; his critics recall the executions at La Cabaña that he oversaw.

personas/fidel-castro/resumen.texto: Lawyer who attacked the Moncada Barracks in 1953 and led the revolution that overthrew Batista in 1959. He ruled Cuba until 2008 with a one-party regime aligned with the USSR; his supporters highlight literacy and public health, and his critics the lack of freedoms and the political prisoners.

personas/horkheimer/resumen.texto: Director from 1930 of the Institute for Social Research in Frankfurt, he formulated the program of “critical theory”. In exile in the United States, he wrote Dialectic of Enlightenment with Adorno, and he reopened the institute in Frankfurt in 1950.

personas/adorno/resumen.texto: Frankfurt School philosopher who criticized the “culture industry” and instrumental reason. Co-author of Dialectic of Enlightenment and The Authoritarian Personality (1950).

personas/marcuse/resumen.texto: Frankfurt School philosopher based in the United States. One-Dimensional Man (1964) made him a reference point for the New Left and the students of 1968.

personas/paulo-freire/resumen.texto: Brazilian educator who taught adults to read starting from their own reality. Exiled after the 1964 coup, he wrote Pedagogy of the Oppressed in Chile, the foundation of popular education in Latin America.

personas/sidney-webb/resumen.texto: One of the intellectual founders of the Fabian Society, which sought a gradual socialism through reforms and public administration. With his wife Beatrice he co-founded the London School of Economics (1895), and he drafted Clause IV of the Labour Party (1918).

personas/havel/resumen.texto: Czech playwright, spokesman for Charter 77 and political prisoner of the communist regime. His essay The Power of the Powerless (1978) described life under “post-totalitarianism”; after the Velvet Revolution he was president of Czechoslovakia and then of the Czech Republic.

personas/nyerere/resumen.texto: First president of Tanganyika and then of Tanzania (1961-1985). With the Arusha Declaration (1967) he promoted the “African socialism” of ujamaa villages, whose forced relocation of peasants and poor economic results were the main criticism.

personas/proudhon/resumen.texto: French printer, the first to call himself an anarchist. In What Is Property? (1840) he answered “property is theft”; he proposed mutualism, free credit and a federation of free associations in place of the state.

personas/stirner/resumen.texto: Philosopher of the Young Hegelians of Berlin. In The Ego and Its Own (1844) he rejected the state, religion and any abstract idea imposed on the individual; he is the forerunner of individualist anarchism.

personas/bakunin/resumen.texto: Russian revolutionary who took part in the insurrections of 1848 and escaped from Siberia. In the First International he led the anti-authoritarian current against Marx and was expelled at the Hague Congress (1872); he is one of the founders of collectivist anarchism.

personas/kropotkin/resumen.texto: Russian prince and geographer who renounced his title and spent decades in exile in England. A theorist of anarcho-communism (The Conquest of Bread, 1892), he argued in Mutual Aid (1902) that cooperation is as important a factor in evolution as competition.

personas/malatesta/resumen.texto: Italian anarchist of the anti-authoritarian International, persecuted and exiled for half a century. He lived in Buenos Aires from 1885 to 1889, where he revived La Questione Sociale and promoted the first workers' societies; he died under fascist house arrest in Rome.

personas/emma-goldman/resumen.texto: Anarchist born in Kaunas who emigrated to the United States, she edited the magazine Mother Earth and championed freedom of speech, birth control and women's emancipation. Deported to Soviet Russia in 1919, she left disillusioned and criticized Bolshevism.

personas/tolstoi/resumen.texto: Author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina who, after his religious crisis, preached a Christianity of nonviolence and rejection of the state, the official Church and property. The Kingdom of God Is Within You (1894) influenced Gandhi, with whom he corresponded.

personas/sorel/resumen.texto: French engineer who theorized revolutionary syndicalism and the “myth” of the general strike in Reflections on Violence (1908). He influenced both the syndicalist left and Mussolini and early fascism.

personas/flores-magon/resumen.texto: Oaxacan journalist and opponent of Porfirio Díaz through the newspaper Regeneración. In exile in the United States, he led the Mexican Liberal Party (1906 program) and moved toward anarchism; he died in prison at Leavenworth penitentiary.

personas/durruti/resumen.texto: Anarchist militant of the CNT and the FAI who lived in Argentina, Chile and other countries in the 1920s. When the civil war broke out in 1936 he led the column that set out from Barcelona for Aragon, and he died on the Madrid front that same year.

personas/nordau/resumen.texto: Physician and cultural critic born in Pest, known for Degeneration (1892). He was Herzl's chief ally, vice-president of the first Zionist congresses and author of the Basel Program.

personas/borojov/resumen.texto: Theorist of socialist Zionism and founder of Poale Zion. He argued that the Jewish proletariat needed a territory of its own in order to integrate into the economy and wage the class struggle, and that this territory should be the Land of Israel.

personas/a-d-gordon/resumen.texto: Labor Zionist thinker who emigrated to Palestine at the age of 48 to work the land. He preached the “religion of labor”: Jewish national renewal through manual and agricultural work, a central idea of the kibbutz movement.

personas/tocqueville/resumen.texto: French magistrate who traveled to the United States in 1831 and wrote Democracy in America. He warned of the “tyranny of the majority” and the soft despotism of a tutelary state; he was also a deputy and Minister of Foreign Affairs in 1849.

personas/mussolini/resumen.texto: A socialist expelled from the party in 1914 for supporting Italy's entry into the war, he founded the Fasci di Combattimento (1919). He came to power after the March on Rome (1922) and established a one-party dictatorship; an ally of Hitler, he was removed from power in 1943 and shot by partisans in 1945.

personas/gentile/resumen.texto: Idealist philosopher, Mussolini's Minister of Education (1922-1924) and the chief ideologue of fascism. He wrote the Manifesto of the Fascist Intellectuals and the philosophical part of The Doctrine of Fascism; he was killed by partisans in Florence in 1944.

personas/croce/resumen.texto: Italian liberal philosopher and historian, a central figure of Italian culture in his time. In 1925 he wrote the Manifesto of the Anti-Fascist Intellectuals in response to Gentile.

personas/hitler/resumen.texto: Leader of the National Socialist Party, he wrote Mein Kampf in prison after the failed Munich putsch (1923). Chancellor from 1933, he established a totalitarian dictatorship, unleashed the Second World War and ordered the extermination of the Jews of Europe; he committed suicide in Berlin in 1945.

personas/carl-schmitt/resumen.texto: German jurist who defined the political by the friend–enemy distinction and the sovereign as he who decides on the state of exception. He joined the Nazi Party in 1933 and provided legal justification for the regime; his work remains debated on both the left and the right.

personas/arendt/resumen.texto: German Jewish philosopher who fled Nazism and settled in New York. In The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951) she analyzed Nazism and Stalinism as a new form of domination, and in Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963) she coined the phrase “banality of evil”.

personas/popper/resumen.texto: Austrian-British philosopher who proposed falsifiability as the criterion of science. In exile in New Zealand, he wrote The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945), in which he criticized the philosophies of Plato, Hegel and Marx as roots of totalitarianism.

personas/isaiah-berlin/resumen.texto: Riga-born British philosopher, professor at Oxford. He distinguished “negative” liberty (absence of interference) from “positive” liberty (self-government) and defended value pluralism against systems that promise a final harmony.

personas/gandhi/resumen.texto: Indian lawyer who developed satyagraha, nonviolent civil resistance, in South Africa. From 1915 he led the movement for Indian independence; he was assassinated in 1948 by a Hindu nationalist.

personas/sukarno/resumen.texto: Leader of Indonesian nationalism who proclaimed independence in 1945 and was the country's first president. Host of the Bandung Conference (1955), he ruled in an increasingly authoritarian manner until Suharto displaced him in 1967.

personas/cesaire/resumen.texto: Martinican poet, one of the creators of the Négritude movement in Paris in the 1930s. He was mayor of Fort-de-France for more than half a century and wrote Discourse on Colonialism (1950).

personas/fanon/resumen.texto: Martinican psychiatrist who worked at the Blida hospital in Algeria and joined the National Liberation Front. He analyzed the psychological effects of colonialism and justified anticolonial violence in The Wretched of the Earth (1961).

personas/nkrumah/resumen.texto: Leader of the independence of the Gold Coast, which in 1957 became Ghana, the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence. He promoted Pan-Africanism; from 1964 he ruled under a one-party system and was overthrown in a coup in 1966.

personas/martin-luther-king/resumen.texto: Baptist minister who led the African American civil rights movement with nonviolent methods, from the Montgomery boycott (1955) to the March on Washington (1963). Awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964, he was assassinated in Memphis in 1968.

personas/malcolm-x/resumen.texto: Spokesman for the Nation of Islam who advocated Black nationalism and self-defense rather than nonviolent integration. He broke with that organization in 1964, traveled to Mecca and moderated part of his rhetoric; he was assassinated in New York in 1965.

personas/rosa-parks/resumen.texto: Seamstress and NAACP activist who on December 1, 1955, refused to give up her seat to a white man on a Montgomery bus. Her arrest triggered the boycott that propelled the civil rights movement.

personas/mandela/resumen.texto: Leader of the African National Congress who turned to armed struggle after the Sharpeville massacre and was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1964. Released in 1990 after 27 years in prison, he negotiated the end of apartheid with de Klerk and was the first president elected by universal suffrage (1994-1999).

personas/de-klerk/resumen.texto: Last white president of South Africa (1989-1994). He legalized the African National Congress, released Mandela in 1990 and negotiated the transition; he shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with him.

personas/olympe-de-gouges/resumen.texto: French playwright who in 1791 wrote the Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen. An opponent of the Jacobins, she was guillotined in 1793.

personas/wollstonecraft/resumen.texto: English writer who in A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) demanded for women the same rational education as for men. She died after giving birth to her daughter, the future Mary Shelley.

personas/lucretia-mott/resumen.texto: Quaker preacher and abolitionist from Philadelphia. With Elizabeth Cady Stanton she organized the Seneca Falls Convention (1848).

personas/elizabeth-cady-stanton/resumen.texto: American abolitionist and suffragist, author of the Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments (1848). With Susan B. Anthony she led the campaign for women's suffrage for decades.

personas/emmeline-pankhurst/resumen.texto: Founder in 1903 of the Women's Social and Political Union, which campaigned for women's suffrage in Britain through direct action, hunger strikes and damage to property. British women over 30 could vote from 1918, and on equal terms with men from 1928, the year of her death.

personas/beauvoir/resumen.texto: French existentialist philosopher and novelist, Sartre's companion. The Second Sex (1949) analyzed how woman was constructed as man's “Other” and is one of the founding works of feminism in the second half of the 20th century.

personas/betty-friedan/resumen.texto: American journalist whose book The Feminine Mystique (1963) spurred the second wave of feminism. She co-founded and presided over the National Organization for Women (NOW, 1966).

personas/ellul/resumen.texto: A professor in Bordeaux and a Protestant, he argued in The Technological Society (1954) that technique had become an autonomous system that imposes its logic on society. He influenced environmentalism and critics of technology.

personas/rachel-carson/resumen.texto: Marine biologist with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and science writer. Silent Spring (1962) denounced the harm caused by synthetic pesticides and gave rise to the modern environmental movement.

personas/garrett-hardin/resumen.texto: American ecologist, author of the article “The Tragedy of the Commons” (1968). He advocated population control and restrictive positions on immigration that were widely criticized.

personas/donella-meadows/resumen.texto: MIT scientist, lead author of The Limits to Growth (1972), the report to the Club of Rome that modeled the clash between growth and the planet's finite resources.

personas/brundtland/resumen.texto: Physician and prime minister of Norway for three terms. She chaired the World Commission on Environment and Development, whose report Our Common Future (1987) defined “sustainable development”.

personas/kaczynski/resumen.texto: Mathematician who left teaching at Berkeley and isolated himself in a cabin in Montana. Between 1978 and 1995 he sent bombs that killed three people and injured twenty-three (“Unabomber”); he was arrested in 1996 after the publication of his manifesto, pleaded guilty and was sentenced to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

personas/pio-xi/resumen.texto: Pope from 1922. He signed the Lateran Pacts with Italy (1929), published Quadragesimo anno (1931) and condemned Nazism in Mit brennender Sorge (1937) and communism in Divini Redemptoris (1937).

personas/gustavo-gutierrez/resumen.texto: Peruvian Dominican priest whose A Theology of Liberation (1971) gave its name to a current that reads the Gospel from the “preferential option for the poor”. The Vatican criticized his use of Marxist categories in 1984; in 2018 Francis congratulated him on his work.

personas/laclau/resumen.texto: Argentine philosopher, professor at the University of Essex. With Mouffe he developed a “post-Marxist” theory of hegemony, and in On Populist Reason (2005) he described populism as a logic for constructing a “people”; he was close to Kirchnerism.

personas/chantal-mouffe/resumen.texto: Belgian philosopher, co-author with Laclau of Hegemony and Socialist Strategy (1985). She advocates an “agonistic” democracy, with conflict between legitimate adversaries, and a “left populism”.

personas/fukuyama/resumen.texto: American political scientist who in 1989, while at the State Department, argued that liberal democracy was the “end of history” as a form of government. He later distanced himself from neoconservatism and studied state-building and political identity.

personas/negri/resumen.texto: Italian philosopher of operaismo and workers' autonomy, convicted in Italy for his links to Autonomia groups accused of political violence, charges he always denied; he lived in exile in France between 1983 and 1997. With Hardt he wrote Empire (2000), on a networked global sovereignty.

personas/michael-hardt/resumen.texto: American philosopher, professor at Duke University, co-author with Negri of Empire (2000), Multitude (2004) and Commonwealth (2009).

personas/walesa/resumen.texto: Electrician at the Gdansk shipyards who led the 1980 strikes and the Solidarity trade union. Awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983, he was president of Poland between 1990 and 1995.

hechos/revoluciones-de-1848/resumen.texto: Wave of revolutions that began in Paris in February 1848 and spread to Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Budapest and other cities, with liberal, national and social demands. It was defeated almost everywhere by 1849, but it ended serfdom in Austria and left universal male suffrage in France.

hechos/convencion-de-seneca-falls/resume.texto: First women's rights convention in the United States, convened on July 19 and 20, 1848, by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott. It approved the Declaration of Sentiments and, by a narrow margin, the demand for women's suffrage.

hechos/primera-internacional/resumen.texto: The International Workingmen's Association was founded in London on September 28, 1864, and brought together British trade unionists, French mutualists, Marxists and anarchists. It split at the 1872 Hague Congress with the expulsion of Bakunin and was dissolved in 1876.

hechos/comuna-de-paris/resumen.texto: Revolutionary government of Paris between March 18 and May 28, 1871, after the French defeat by Prussia. It separated Church and State and adopted social measures; it was crushed by the Versailles army during the “Bloody Week”, with thousands executed by firing squad.

hechos/revuelta-de-haymarket/resumen.texto: During the strike for the eight-hour day, on May 4, 1886, a bomb exploded among the police at a rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square, followed by a shootout with deaths on both sides. Eight anarchists were convicted without proof that they had thrown the bomb, and four were hanged in 1887; in 1893 the governor pardoned the survivors. The Second International made May 1 Workers' Day in their memory.

hechos/segunda-internacional/resumen.texto: Federation of socialist and labor parties founded in Paris on July 14, 1889, dominated by German social democracy. It proclaimed May Day and split in 1914, when most of its parties supported their governments in the war.

hechos/fundacion-del-bund/resumen.texto: The General Jewish Labour Bund in Lithuania, Poland and Russia was founded in Vilna in October 1897, the same year as the First Zionist Congress. Socialist and non-Zionist, it advocated Yiddish-language cultural autonomy for Jews in the countries where they lived; it was the main Jewish party in Poland between the wars.

hechos/segundo-congreso-del-posdr/resume.texto: At the second congress of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party, which opened in Brussels and moved to London in 1903, the supporters of Lenin and of a closed party of militants prevailed in a vote and called themselves Bolsheviks (“majoritarians”); Martov's supporters became the Mensheviks.

hechos/revolucion-mexicana/resumen.texto: Revolution that began against the reelection of Porfirio Díaz in 1910 and continued as a civil war among caudillos such as Madero, Villa, Zapata and Carranza. It produced the Constitution of 1917, with land reform and labor rights.

hechos/revolucion-rusa/resumen.texto: In February 1917 (March in the Western calendar), strikes and mutinies in Petrograd led to the abdication of Nicholas II and the end of the monarchy. The provisional government coexisted with the soviets until the Bolsheviks seized power in October.

hechos/revolucion-de-octubre/resumen.texto: On October 25, 1917 (November 7 in the Western calendar), the Bolsheviks, directed from the Smolny Institute, took the Winter Palace and deposed the provisional government. It led to the civil war and the first communist state.

hechos/internacional-comunista/resumen.texto: Worldwide organization of communist parties founded in Moscow in March 1919 on Lenin's initiative. Its 21 Conditions of 1920 separated communists from socialists; Stalin subordinated it to Soviet foreign policy and dissolved it in 1943.

hechos/levantamiento-espartaquista/resum.texto: General strike and communist insurrection in Berlin in January 1919, in the midst of the German Revolution. The Social Democratic government suppressed it with the Freikorps, who murdered Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht on January 15.

hechos/marcha-sobre-roma/resumen.texto: In late October 1922, thousands of fascist Blackshirts advanced on Rome. King Victor Emmanuel III refused to declare a state of siege and entrusted the government to Mussolini, who from there gradually built his dictatorship.

hechos/marcha-de-la-sal/resumen.texto: Between March 12 and April 6, 1930, Gandhi walked with his followers some 390 kilometers from the Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi to make salt in defiance of the British monopoly. It sparked a civil disobedience campaign with tens of thousands imprisoned.

hechos/ascenso-de-hitler/resumen.texto: On January 30, 1933, President Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor. Within a few months, through the decree issued after the Reichstag fire and the Enabling Act, the government suppressed political parties, trade unions and civil liberties.

hechos/gran-purga/resumen.texto: Stalin's campaign of repression against party leaders, military officers, minorities and ordinary citizens, with the Moscow trials as a showcase. According to secret police records, some 680,000 people were shot in 1937 and 1938, and hundreds of thousands were sent to the Gulag.

hechos/revolucion-espanola-de-1936/resum.texto: When the military coup of July 1936 failed in Barcelona, the anarchist CNT and FAI collectivized factories and land in Catalonia, Aragon and other Republican areas. Clashes with communists and republicans, such as the May Days of 1937, and Franco's victory in 1939 brought it to an end.

hechos/revolucion-china/resumen.texto: After the civil war against the Kuomintang, the People's Liberation Army took Beijing and Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China on October 1, 1949. Chiang Kai-shek's government withdrew to Taiwan.

hechos/boicot-de-montgomery/resumen.texto: After Rosa Parks's arrest, African Americans in Montgomery stopped riding the buses for 381 days, led by Martin Luther King. It ended when the Supreme Court confirmed that segregation in public transportation was unconstitutional.
